title: FINSEC Dialog Conversation with Mohnish Pabrai
summary: A Twitter Spaces conversation with Sandeep Parekh covering the origins and economics of Dakshana, why Pabrai ignores macro and focuses on micro anomalies, the dot-com era funeral home and Silicon Valley Bank trades, his Turkish warehouse investment, and the painful lesson of selling Kotak and Blue Dart too early. Main takeaways: no leverage, no shorting, patience and holding periods matter most, and compounding over a long runway makes even 7-9% returns transformative.

ideas.idea: Large inheritances do more harm than good, so surplus assets must be recycled back to society rather than given to the gene pool.
ideas.detail: Bestowing large amounts on children is like an IV drip that puts them in a welfare state; Buffett's line that Jesse Owens' son should start at the 10-meter line but not the 40-meter line.

ideas.idea: Philanthropy inverts the investing rule: you must go high risk, swing for the fences and be fully willing to fail, because that is the only way to move the needle.
ideas.detail: In investing he goes low risk, high return and can let 99.9% of the market go by; in philanthropy you are forced to confront tough problems like poverty and education. He started giving 2% of assets a year, modelled on Buffett giving 5% of his Berkshire shares annually.

ideas.idea: Dakshana was cloned from Anand Kumar's Super 30 and scaled from 30 kids to over 1,000 a year, with 60-80% admitted to IITs, AIIMS or medical schools at $2,500-3,000 per kid.
ideas.detail: Students come from illiterate rural farming families earning under $100 a month; alumni now work at Microsoft, Amazon and Google, in the IAS, and as VC-funded founders. He started Dakshana at 42 because waiting until 70 or 80 would leave no energy to do more than write checks.

ideas.idea: Micro factors that affect a business directly matter far more to an investor than macro considerations like interest rates or government policy.
ideas.detail: Many long-listed businesses have done well regardless of the economy; if you can figure out the three main factors that drive a business's outcome, that is what matters. He does not try to answer macro questions because he has no better answer than anyone else.

ideas.idea: Bubbles are extremely common because humans vacillate between fear and greed, and at extremes like 1999-2000 the euphoria becomes obvious.
ideas.detail: In early 2000 Microsoft was among the three largest market caps at over $600 billion, trading at 70-80x earnings; he told Microsoft employees with 90% of net worth in the stock that everything has a price. He recommends Ron Insana's book TrendWatching on bubbles. The day NASDAQ peaked, March 9, 2000, Berkshire hit a multi-year low.

ideas.idea: In 2022 crypto, GameStop and AMC are bubbles, but the overall market is not as extreme as 1999-2000 and he has no bets in those areas.
ideas.detail: All bubbles have a kernel of truth at the core; frothiness in part of tech has corrected somewhat. He saw the dot-com crash but did not see the severity of the financial crisis until it was well underway.

ideas.idea: Pabrai Funds did 70% in its first year through the dot-com crash and 20-40% a year after by buying non-sexy businesses like funeral homes at 2x earnings and steel mills at 3x.
ideas.detail: Stewart Enterprises had a $200 million market cap, a billion in debt, yet produced $100 million a year in cash after debt service; it sold its European business for about $500 million to pay down debt and was a multi-bagger within 12-18 months. He found it on Value Line's low-PE list.

ideas.idea: Funeral homes and 'recycling' businesses have great economics: the lowest failure rate of any US business, predictable demand, no price shopping and limited competition.
ideas.detail: Nobody knows who will die in St. Louis next year but the number is precise; 22-year-olds do not aspire to the funeral business. TJ Maxx buying surplus clothing and Delaware bankruptcy lawyers are other examples of recycling businesses; India's NCLT is building a similar system.

ideas.idea: Cloning is the great shortcut in a universe of 50,000 stocks: start with what investors you admire have already put their own money into.
ideas.detail: Munger endorses cloning; a great investor's portfolio has already passed one filter. His Turkish investments came from spending a week visiting every company a Ben Graham-style friend in Istanbul owned.

ideas.idea: His Turkish warehouse and logistics company was bought for $7 million (one third of the company) at a $20 million market cap against $700 million to $1.5 billion of liquidation value.
ideas.detail: 12 million square feet of 99%-leased prime warehouses with tenants like Amazon, Ikea, Carrefour and DuPont, plus Turkey's largest freight rail and truck operator. Bought at 5 lira to the dollar; despite the lira going to 17, the investment is up 5x in dollars because steel, concrete and land have international prices. Turkish retail investors hold for nine days on average, a dream market for value investors.

ideas.idea: Never use leverage and never short, because auction-driven markets swing wildly and you must be able to play the next day.
ideas.detail: Any NSE/BSE stock's 52-week range may be 100 to 300 rupees while a Mumbai flat barely moves 10% in a year. Shorting caps the upside at a double and the downside at bankruptcy; the hedge funds shorting GameStop and AMC analyzed correctly but are gone.

ideas.idea: Investing is not a game where the highest IQ wins; temperament and patience matter most, and holding periods are the lesson he is still learning.
ideas.detail: The Turkish company needed only a 100-120 IQ to see it was cheap; what was needed was willingness to buy when others would not and to hold for a very long time.

ideas.idea: Selling Kotak, Blue Dart and Sky Pack in 2000 for no reason was the biggest lesson of his career: Kotak went up 500x and Blue Dart 300x after he sold.
ideas.detail: In 1995 he put $20,000 in India: $10,000 in Satyam at 40 rupees, which he sold near 6,000-7,000 rupees for $1.3-1.5 million within 10% of the top, and $3,000 each in Blue Dart, Sky Pack and Kotak, which were flat and he sold anyway. Sky Pack fell 90%, but three of four were 100-baggers or more. 'The most important skill is to be patient.'

ideas.idea: Inactivity wins: the Fidelity study found the best-performing self-directed accounts belonged to customers who were dead.
ideas.detail: Accounts with hardly any activity did best, and many of the very best had owners who were no longer alive.

ideas.idea: Silicon Valley Bank, his first Pabrai Funds purchase on July 1, 1999, was sold after 2.5x in a year, but it compounded at about 26% a year from 1999 to 2022 because he failed to appreciate how well run the franchise was.
ideas.detail: SVB traded near book value with an undisclosed basket of warrants from venture-backed borrowers; he put 10% of the $1 million fund in. 'Old too soon and wise too late', but investing is a forgiving business where things work out despite many mistakes.

ideas.idea: He is not interested in doubling his money; he wants businesses he can hold 10-20 years for 30x, 50x or 100x, which he cannot find in the US in 2022 but can in a sliver of Turkish companies.
ideas.detail: He invested this way in 1995, switched to cheap stocks in 1999-2000 when things got euphoric, and should have switched back to compounders in 2009. In the US even after corrections he finds it hard to see 5-10x in 5-10 years.

ideas.idea: The investor's job description is reading and thinking, not acting; actions should be very infrequent and curiosity makes it a great life rather than work.
ideas.detail: Tom Murphy of Capital Cities said he never worked a day in his life; visiting 15 businesses in a week in Turkey is more fun than sightseeing.

ideas.idea: Buffett's Japanese trading house bet, financed entirely with yen debt at 0.5% against 7-8% dividend yields, is a way to soak up excess brain horsepower without harming Berkshire.
ideas.detail: About $6-7 billion in 5-10% stakes, up 50-70% in three years, with infinite return on equity invested. Munger told him Buffett's large brain must stay active in ways not detrimental to Berkshire: bridge, Korean stocks bought one Saturday afternoon, negative-rate bonds. Pabrai plays 8-10 hours of bridge a week and has Dakshana for the same reason.

ideas.idea: His approach is not scalable; all investors do worse as assets grow, and Berkshire now needs $30-50 billion positions to move the needle.
ideas.detail: With $500 billion he could not be the same investor; the universe shrinks to companies over $20-30 billion in market cap where a 10% stake is possible.

ideas.idea: Three variables control eventual wealth, in order of importance: length of runway, rate of return, and starting capital; 7-9% returns over a long runway are nothing to look down on.
ideas.detail: Buffett's Manhattan Indians example: $20 in 1622 at 7% becomes $20 trillion by 2022, and $0.02 in 1522 would do the same. Buffett's one wish is that people look at his corpse and say 'man, he was old'; he started at 11 and is 91. The S&P has returned about 9% for 100+ years.

ideas.idea: Being an outsider taught by Buffett, Munger and Graham through the public domain was a gift; he would have done worse in the professional investment industry.
ideas.detail: He never worked under anyone in investing. Becoming an investor was luck: picking up a Peter Lynch book in London in 1994 while running an IT company led him to Buffett biographies. Nick Sleep is miles ahead of him as an investor.

ideas.idea: India has strong long-term tailwinds and is a good place to be, but red tape and constraints on free enterprise leave obvious low-hanging fruit unpicked compared with China.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: He noted at the 2022 Berkshire meeting that Buffett and Munger see non-zero, perhaps 1-5%, odds of a Russian nuclear event, an example of why macro is too hard; global dollar-cost averaging over a long runway is probably the best default.

ideas.idea: He does not invest top-down from hot sectors; he looks for anomalies where value is so compelling that returns come even without growth.
ideas.detail: Indian IT services and cloud will do well, but knowing a sector grows does not mean you can make money. The Turkish bet would return 30x just from reaching fair value even if management did nothing, and they are good capital allocators.

ideas.idea: Whatever criteria you set among 50,000 global stocks (net-nets, PE of one, 100-baggers) you will find if you stay focused; he has chosen the multi-bagger game.
ideas.detail: Real net-nets can still work, but dot-com era net-nets were illusions because they were bleeding cash daily. Net-nets are no longer an area of interest for him.
